**[I. Executive Summary]{.underline}**

Thornfield Advisory Group (\"Thornfield\") was engaged by Clearview Health Partners LLC (\"Clearview\") and Clearview Health Partners Fund IV, L.P. (\"Fund IV,\" and together with Clearview, the \"Client\") to perform a quality of earnings analysis of Pinnacle Medical Group, P.A. (\"Pinnacle\" or the \"Company\") in connection with the proposed acquisition of Pinnacle by Clearview HC Acquisition Sub, Inc. (\"Merger Sub\"), a wholly owned subsidiary of Clearview HC Holdings, LLC, which is itself controlled by Fund IV. The proposed transaction is structured as a reverse triangular merger in which Merger Sub will merge with and into Pinnacle, with Pinnacle surviving as the post-closing operating entity.

**Scope.** Thornfield\'s analysis covers Pinnacle\'s historical financial performance for fiscal years ended December 31, 2022, December 31, 2023, and December 31, 2024, with primary focus on fiscal year 2024 (\"FY 2024\"). Our review was based on audited financial statements for all three fiscal years as prepared by Stonebridge & Wills CPAs, management-prepared monthly financial data, general ledger detail, revenue cycle reports from Apex Practice Solutions LLC (Pinnacle\'s revenue cycle management vendor), payer contracts and fee schedules, payroll and benefits data, lease agreements and occupancy cost data, and management interviews. Principal management interviews were conducted with Dr. Raymond Vasquez, Founder and majority shareholder; Janet Morales, Vice President of Human Resources and Chief Compliance Officer; and division chiefs across Pinnacle\'s primary service lines.

**Key Conclusions.** Based on the procedures performed, Thornfield has reached the following principal conclusions:

1\. Pinnacle\'s reported FY 2024 revenue of \$187.3 million is supportable, with only minor reclassification observations between service lines that do not affect total revenue or EBITDA.

2\. Pinnacle\'s reported FY 2024 EBITDA of \$25.6 million is materially accurate based on our analysis of the Company\'s audited financial statements and supporting general ledger detail.

3\. Thornfield identified pro forma EBITDA adjustments totaling \$3.97 million, consisting of above-market founder compensation normalization, one-time EHR system migration costs, a one-time litigation settlement, and defunct clinic wind-down costs. These adjustments yield an **Adjusted EBITDA of \$29.57 million** for FY 2024.

4\. Several areas warrant further diligence attention, including related-party transactions involving Dr. Vasquez and his affiliated entities, revenue concentration by government payer, near-term lease expirations at revenue-significant clinic locations, and occupancy cost normalization for above-market related-party leases.

**Transaction Overview.** The proposed transaction is structured as a reverse triangular merger. Per the executed Letter of Intent dated September 15, 2024, the Base Enterprise Value is \$224.8 million, which represents approximately 7.6x Thornfield\'s calculated Adjusted EBITDA of \$29.57 million. Net Debt as of the expected measurement date is estimated at \$31.2 million, yielding an estimated Equity Value of approximately \$195.1 million. The consideration mix consists of approximately 80% cash and 20% rollover equity, with an additional earnout component of up to \$20.0 million tied to calendar year 2025 and 2026 revenue targets.

**[II. Scope and Methodology]{.underline}**

**Engagement Date and Scope Period.** Thornfield was formally engaged in October 2024 following the execution of the Letter of Intent between the parties on September 15, 2024. Our analysis covers the three most recently completed fiscal years --- FY 2022 (ended December 31, 2022), FY 2023 (ended December 31, 2023), and FY 2024 (ended December 31, 2024). Our primary focus is on FY 2024 financial results as the most recent completed period and the basis for the transaction\'s Adjusted EBITDA.

**Data Sources.** In performing our analysis, Thornfield reviewed and relied upon the following data sources and materials:

> \(a\) Audited financial statements for FY 2022, FY 2023, and FY 2024, including accompanying notes and audit opinions, prepared by Stonebridge & Wills CPAs, Pinnacle\'s independent auditor;
>
> \(b\) Monthly management profit and loss statements for FY 2023 and FY 2024, including department-level and clinic-level detail;
>
> \(c\) General ledger detail for FY 2024, including account-level transaction records;
>
> \(d\) Revenue cycle management reports generated by Apex Practice Solutions LLC (\"Apex\"), Pinnacle\'s outsourced RCM vendor, including payer remittance summaries, denial rate analyses, and collection rate data;
>
> \(e\) Payer contracts and fee schedules for Pinnacle\'s principal commercial insurance and government payer arrangements;
>
> \(f\) Payroll and benefits data, including physician and advanced practice provider compensation records, bonus calculations, and benefits costs;
>
> \(g\) Lease agreements and occupancy cost data for all fourteen (14) clinic locations operated by Pinnacle; and
>
> \(h\) Management interviews conducted with Dr. Raymond Vasquez (Founder and Chief Executive Officer), Janet Morales (Vice President of Human Resources and Chief Compliance Officer), and division chiefs for orthopedics, pain management, cardiology, and primary care.

**Methodology.** Thornfield\'s analysis involved the following procedures: We analyzed Pinnacle\'s reported EBITDA for each fiscal year under review and identified adjustments categorized as (i) non-recurring items, (ii) non-operational items, and (iii) owner-related adjustments, to derive a normalized or Adjusted EBITDA. We reviewed revenue quality by examining payer mix composition, service line revenue distribution, and clinic-level revenue contribution. We assessed the sustainability of reported earnings by examining key cost drivers, including physician compensation, occupancy costs, RCM vendor fees, and administrative overhead. We evaluated net working capital components as of the expected closing date and compared them to the trailing twelve-month average target established in the Letter of Intent. We also reviewed debt and debt-like items to confirm the components of Net Debt used in the equity value bridge.

**Limitations.** This report is a summary of Thornfield\'s quality of earnings analysis and does not constitute an audit, review, or compilation of Pinnacle\'s financial statements in accordance with standards promulgated by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. Thornfield has relied upon the representations of Pinnacle\'s management and upon data and documents provided by Pinnacle, its advisors, and its independent auditor, Stonebridge & Wills CPAs, without independent verification of all underlying records. Certain observations contained herein relate to regulatory compliance, legal matters, and tax matters, which are noted for informational purposes only and are beyond the scope of Thornfield\'s financial engagement. This report is intended solely for use by Clearview, Fund IV, and their legal advisors (including Linden, Ashby & Whitmore LLP) and should not be relied upon by any third party for any purpose.

**[III. Revenue Analysis]{.underline}**

**III.A. Historical Revenue Summary**

The following table summarizes Pinnacle\'s reported revenue for the three fiscal years under review:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Metric**              **FY 2022**       **FY 2023**       **FY 2024**
  ----------------------- ----------------- ----------------- -----------------
  Total Revenue           \$158.7M          \$172.1M          \$187.3M

  Year-over-Year Growth   ---               8.4%              8.8%
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pinnacle has demonstrated consistent revenue growth over the period analyzed, with a three-year compound annual growth rate (\"CAGR\") of approximately 8.6%. Revenue growth has been driven by a combination of same-clinic volume increases across established locations, the addition of two new clinic locations (one opened in the second half of FY 2023 and one in early FY 2024), and modest rate increases achieved through commercial payer contract renegotiations completed during FY 2023 and FY 2024.

The FY 2024 revenue figure of \$187.3 million is derived from Pinnacle\'s audited financial statements as prepared by Stonebridge & Wills CPAs. Thornfield reviewed the revenue figure against general ledger detail, monthly management P&L reports, and Apex Practice Solutions revenue cycle summaries and found no material discrepancies. We noted minor reclassification observations between certain service lines (primarily between ancillary services and the primary service line under which those services were originally coded), but these reclassifications do not affect total reported revenue or EBITDA.

**III.B. Revenue by Service Line**

Pinnacle operates across five principal service lines. The following table summarizes the breakdown of FY 2024 revenue by service line:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Service Line**                    **FY 2024 Revenue**     **% of Total**
  ----------------------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------
  Orthopedics                         \$65.6M                 35.0%

  Pain Management                     \$46.8M                 25.0%

  Cardiology                          \$37.5M                 20.0%

  Primary Care                        \$28.1M                 15.0%

  Ancillary Services (MRI, Lab, PT)   \$9.3M                  5.0%

  **Total**                           **\$187.3M**            **100.0%**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Orthopedics is Pinnacle\'s largest service line, contributing \$65.6 million, or 35.0% of total revenue, in FY 2024. Pain management is the second-largest service line at \$46.8 million, or 25.0% of total revenue. Together, orthopedics and pain management constitute approximately 60% of Pinnacle\'s total revenue, reflecting the Company\'s historical focus on musculoskeletal and interventional services.

Cardiology and primary care contribute 20.0% and 15.0% of revenue, respectively, and represent growth areas for the practice. Ancillary services --- including magnetic resonance imaging (\"MRI\"), laboratory, and physical therapy --- contribute \$9.3 million, or 5.0% of total revenue. Thornfield notes that a portion of ancillary services revenue involves related-party arrangements between Pinnacle and entities in which Dr. Vasquez holds partial ownership interests. The economic terms and regulatory compliance posture of these arrangements are discussed further in Section VII.

Government payer revenue --- consisting of Medicare, Medicaid, and TRICARE --- represents approximately 51% of Pinnacle\'s total revenue. Medicare is the single largest payer at 34.0%, which is consistent with industry norms for a multi-specialty physician group with a significant orthopedic and cardiology practice serving an aging patient population in metropolitan Texas and Oklahoma markets.

The concentration of government payer revenue subjects Pinnacle to heightened regulatory requirements, including compliance obligations under the Physician Self-Referral Law (the \"Stark Law\"), the federal Anti-Kickback Statute, and the False Claims Act. Additionally, the concentration in government payers exposes Pinnacle to reimbursement rate changes driven by annual CMS rulemaking, particularly with respect to the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule and related payment methodologies.

Pinnacle\'s three Oklahoma clinic locations derive a significant portion of their Medicaid revenue from contracts with SoonerSelect managed care organizations. These MCO contracts are subject to periodic rebidding by the Oklahoma Health Care Authority and rate renegotiation processes that could affect revenue from those locations in future periods. The Oklahoma Medicaid revenue component is included in the \$22.48 million Medicaid figure above.

Commercial insurance represents 40.0% of total revenue, or approximately \$74.92 million. Pinnacle\'s commercial payer portfolio includes contracts with Blue Cross Blue Shield of Texas, Aetna, UnitedHealthcare, and several regional health plans. Self-pay and other revenue of \$16.85 million includes patient responsibility amounts, out-of-network services, and miscellaneous income.

**III.D. Revenue by Clinic Location**

Pinnacle operates fourteen (14) clinic locations across two states --- eleven (11) in Texas and three (3) in Oklahoma. The Texas clinics contribute approximately 82% of total revenue (\$153.6 million), while the Oklahoma clinics contribute approximately 18% (\$33.7 million).

The two highest-revenue Texas clinics are the Fort Worth main campus (Clinic A) and the Plano location. The Plano and Frisco locations together contribute approximately \$28.5 million in annual revenue, representing approximately 15.2% of Pinnacle\'s total FY 2024 revenue.

Thornfield notes that the leases for the Plano and Frisco clinic locations expire in approximately January 2026 and February 2026, respectively --- within approximately eight (8) months of the expected closing date --- with no renewal options available under the current lease agreements. The potential non-renewal or loss of these clinic locations would expose the Company to meaningful revenue disruption. Refer to Section VI for further discussion of lease expirations and associated risks.

The remaining twelve clinic locations are diversified across the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, the greater Oklahoma City area, and the Tulsa corridor. No individual clinic other than the Fort Worth main campus exceeds 12% of total revenue, and the overall geographic diversification within each state provides reasonable protection against localized market disruptions.

**IV.B. Pro Forma EBITDA Adjustments**

Thornfield identified four pro forma adjustments to Pinnacle\'s reported FY 2024 EBITDA. Each adjustment is described below with narrative justification, followed by a summary table.

**Adjustment 1 --- Above-Market Founder Compensation Normalization: \$1.82M**

Dr. Raymond Vasquez, as Founder, majority shareholder, and Chief Executive Officer of Pinnacle, received total compensation (inclusive of base salary, annual bonus, and personal benefits charged to the Company) of approximately \$2.95 million in FY 2024. This level of compensation reflects both Dr. Vasquez\'s clinical role as an orthopedic surgeon and his administrative role as the Company\'s chief executive.

For purposes of this analysis, Thornfield estimated normalized compensation for a physician executive serving as Medical Director and CEO of a multi-specialty group practice of comparable size and complexity. Based on industry benchmarking data sourced from the Medical Group Management Association (\"MGMA\") and SCA Health compensation surveys, Thornfield estimates normalized total compensation for such a role at approximately \$1.13 million. The resulting add-back is calculated as follows: \$2.95 million (actual) less \$1.13 million (normalized) equals \$1.82 million.

Thornfield recommends that the parties confirm the post-closing compensation level for Dr. Vasquez against fair market value benchmarks. The proposed annual Medical Director compensation of \$1.2 million reflected in the draft employment term sheet exceeds the 90th percentile for orthopedic surgeon Medical Directors in comparable metropolitan markets.

**Adjustment 2 --- One-Time EHR System Migration Costs: \$0.95M**

During Q1 and Q2 of FY 2024, Pinnacle incurred \$0.95 million in one-time costs associated with migrating from its legacy electronic health records platform to a new EHR system. These costs included data migration and system integration fees (\$0.38 million), staff training and temporary productivity losses (\$0.32 million), and third-party consultant fees (\$0.25 million). Thornfield deems these expenses non-recurring in nature and appropriate for add-back, as the migration project was completed during FY 2024 and no further material expenditures are anticipated.

**Adjustment 3 --- One-Time Litigation Settlement: \$0.60M**

In FY 2024, Pinnacle settled a wrongful termination claim brought by a former clinic administrator for a total of \$0.60 million, inclusive of legal fees and settlement consideration. Thornfield reviewed the circumstances of this matter and confirmed that it related to a discrete employment dispute rather than a systemic pattern of litigation. No similar pending claims were identified during our review of Pinnacle\'s litigation docket. Thornfield deems this a non-recurring expense appropriate for add-back.

**Adjustment 4 --- Defunct Clinic Wind-Down Costs: \$0.60M**

Pinnacle closed its Denton, Texas clinic in mid-2024 following a strategic review of underperforming locations. The Company incurred \$0.60 million in wind-down costs associated with the closure, including lease termination penalties (\$0.22 million), staff severance payments (\$0.18 million), patient record transfer and administrative costs (\$0.12 million), and furniture, fixture, and equipment disposal (\$0.08 million). As the Denton clinic closure is a completed, non-recurring event, Thornfield deems the associated costs appropriate for add-back.

**[III. Federal Healthcare Program Participation and Billing Compliance]{.underline}**

**[III.A. Overview of Government Payer Mix]{.underline}**

Pinnacle participates in Medicare (Parts A and B), Medicaid (including Oklahoma SoonerSelect managed care), and TRICARE. The Target\'s revenue from government payer programs for fiscal year 2024 totaled approximately \$95.53 million, representing approximately 51% of total revenue of \$187.3 million. The revenue breakdown by government payer is as follows: Medicare contributed approximately \$63.68 million (34% of total revenue); Medicaid contributed approximately \$22.48 million (12% of total revenue); and TRICARE contributed approximately \$9.37 million (5% of total revenue).

Pinnacle holds Medicare provider numbers for each of its fourteen (14) clinic locations (eleven in Texas and three in Oklahoma). Each clinic location maintains a separate CMS-855B enrollment with the applicable Medicare Administrative Contractor (\"MAC\"). The proposed merger will constitute a change of ownership (\"CHOW\") requiring notification to CMS and the applicable MACs, as discussed in greater detail in Section VIII below.

The three Oklahoma clinic locations operate under Oklahoma Medicaid managed care contracts with SoonerSelect managed care organizations. These arrangements are subject to separate CHOW and assignment provisions under the applicable MCO contracts and Oklahoma Health Care Authority regulations.

The high concentration of government payer revenue (51% of total revenue) significantly heightens the regulatory risk profile of this transaction across multiple dimensions, including Stark Law compliance, Anti-Kickback Statute compliance, and False Claims Act exposure. Each dollar of government payer revenue that is attributable to an improper arrangement or billing practice carries potential liability under these statutes.

**[III.B. Potential Overbilling --- Pain Management Division Upcoding]{.underline}**

**Finding.** Pinnacle\'s Q3 2024 internal audit identified potential overbilling in the pain management division related to systematic upcoding of Evaluation and Management (\"E&M\") services. Specifically, the internal audit found that pain management physicians were routinely billing at CPT code 99214 (Level 4 established patient office visit) when the clinical documentation in the medical records supported only CPT code 99213 (Level 3 established patient office visit). The pattern was not isolated to a single provider but was observed across multiple physicians in the pain management division at several Texas clinic locations, suggesting a systemic practice rather than individual physician error.

**Scope of Exposure.** Based on the internal audit\'s extrapolation methodology, the estimated overpayment attributable to the upcoding practice across the 2022 through 2024 period is approximately \$1.8 million. This figure represents the difference between the amounts actually billed and collected at the CPT 99214 rate and the amounts that should have been billed at the CPT 99213 rate, applied across the affected claims during the three-year period. The overbilling appears concentrated in the pain management division, although we note that the internal audit did not extend to other Pinnacle specialty divisions (orthopedics, cardiology, or primary care), leaving open the question of whether similar coding practices exist elsewhere within the organization.

**Current Status.** No voluntary self-disclosure has been made to the OIG under its Self-Disclosure Protocol or to CMS. No qui tam or whistleblower action has been identified in connection with the overbilling; however, we note that qui tam actions filed under the False Claims Act are sealed by the court upon filing and remain under seal during the government\'s investigation period, which may last several years. Accordingly, we cannot confirm the absence of a sealed qui tam action. Janet Morales, in her capacity as part-time Chief Compliance Officer, confirmed during her interview that she was aware of the Q3 2024 internal audit findings but stated that remediation was \"ongoing\" and that a decision regarding voluntary self-disclosure was \"pending management review.\" As of the date of this memorandum --- more than five months after the internal audit findings were first identified --- no self-disclosure has been initiated, no external coding audit has been commissioned, and no repayment has been made.

**Compliance Program Concerns.** The delayed response to a material compliance finding raises significant questions about the effectiveness of Pinnacle\'s compliance program. The fact that the Chief Compliance Officer (Janet Morales) simultaneously serves as Vice President of Human Resources creates a structural concern about independence and capacity. The OIG\'s Compliance Program Guidance for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices recommends that the compliance officer have sufficient authority, independence, and resources to implement the compliance program effectively. A dual-hat arrangement in which the CCO also manages the workforce --- including the very physicians whose billing practices are at issue --- compromises this independence. Furthermore, the compliance program, established in 2019 and updated in 2022, has not been subjected to any external validation or mock audit, which would be expected for an organization of this size generating over \$95 million annually from federal healthcare programs.

**Legal Exposure.** The identified overbilling creates potential liability under the federal False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. §3729 et seq. Under the FCA, each claim submitted to a federal healthcare program that includes a false or fraudulent billing code may give rise to liability for treble damages and per-claim civil penalties (currently ranging from \$13,508 to \$27,018 per claim, as adjusted for inflation). If Pinnacle were to make a voluntary self-disclosure under the OIG\'s Self-Disclosure Protocol, the typical resolution amount is 1.5 times single damages --- yielding a potential settlement of approximately \$2.7 million on \$1.8 million in estimated overpayments. If, however, the overbilling is discovered by the government independently (whether through a qui tam action, a CMS audit, or a Zone Program Integrity Contractor (\"ZPIC\") review) without a prior self-disclosure, the government would be entitled to pursue treble damages (approximately \$5.4 million) plus per-claim penalties. Additionally, sustained overbilling of federal healthcare programs may give rise to permissive or mandatory exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid under 42 U.S.C. §1320a-7, which would be catastrophic for an organization that derives 51% of its revenue from government payers.

**Implications for the Transaction.** The draft merger agreement\'s indemnification framework, as circulated on January 8, 2025, does not include a specific or special indemnity for this known overbilling liability. Under the current draft, losses arising from the overbilling would fall under the general representations and warranties (specifically, the seller\'s representation regarding compliance with healthcare laws and the accuracy of billing practices), subject to the \$1.5 million deductible basket. This means that the Buyer would absorb the first \$1.5 million of this known \$1.8 million exposure before any indemnification obligation of the Seller is triggered --- leaving the Seller responsible for only \$300,000 (the amount exceeding the basket), subject to the general indemnification cap. This allocation is commercially unreasonable for a known, quantified pre-closing liability. Moreover, the representations and warranties insurance policy (\$30 million aggregate limit, \$2.0 million retention) would almost certainly exclude this known matter from coverage, as R&W insurers uniformly exclude from coverage any matters disclosed in the data room or otherwise known to the insured parties at the time of policy inception.

**Recommendation.** We recommend the following actions: (a) demand a specific indemnity for the overbilling exposure from dollar one, structured outside the general basket and general indemnification cap; (b) require Seller to initiate a voluntary self-disclosure to the OIG under its Self-Disclosure Protocol prior to closing, or at minimum prior to a date certain post-closing (with a corresponding escrow or holdback to secure the indemnification obligation); (c) require an independent coding audit of the pain management division by a qualified third-party compliance firm as a condition to closing, with the scope extended to other Pinnacle specialty divisions on a sample basis; and (d) confirm with the R&W insurance broker that this known matter is excluded from the policy and evaluate whether additional tail coverage or a separate indemnity escrow is warranted.

**[III.C. Compliance Program Structure]{.underline}**

As noted above, Janet Morales serves in the dual capacity of Vice President of Human Resources and part-time Chief Compliance Officer. This arrangement is inconsistent with the OIG\'s compliance program guidance, which recommends that the CCO report directly to the chief executive officer or the governing board and not be burdened with conflicting operational responsibilities that could compromise the independence of the compliance function. Ms. Morales\'s dual role creates an inherent tension: as VP of Human Resources, she is responsible for managing the physician and staff workforce, including performance evaluations, compensation administration, and disciplinary decisions, while simultaneously serving as the officer responsible for identifying and investigating potential compliance violations by those same individuals.

The compliance program was originally established in 2019 and updated in 2022. No external compliance assessment, mock audit, or independent program evaluation has been conducted at any time during the compliance program\'s existence. Given Pinnacle\'s significant government payer revenue (51% of total revenue, or approximately \$95.53 million), the identified \$1.8 million overbilling issue in the pain management division, and the Target\'s ongoing OCR investigation, the current compliance infrastructure is plainly inadequate for an organization of this size and risk profile.

We recommend that, post-closing, Buyer appoint a full-time, independent Chief Compliance Officer who reports directly to the board of directors (or its equivalent) and engage an external compliance consulting firm to conduct a comprehensive compliance program assessment covering coding and billing, Stark Law and AKS compliance, HIPAA privacy and security, and operational compliance.

**[IV. Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute Compliance]{.underline}**

**[IV.A. Dr. Vasquez Post-Closing Compensation]{.underline}**

**Finding.** The proposed post-closing employment agreement for Dr. Raymond Vasquez, M.D., which has been circulated in draft form between the parties\' respective counsel, provides for annual compensation of \$1.2 million in Dr. Vasquez\'s capacity as Medical Director of the surviving entity. The proposed employment term is three years following the closing of the merger. Dr. Vasquez is currently age 61 and has indicated his intention to remain in this leadership role through the full three-year term.

**Benchmarking Concern.** Based on our review of available fair market value compensation survey data from the Medical Group Management Association (\"MGMA\"), Sullivan Cotter Associates (\"SCA\"), and the American Medical Group Association (\"AMGA\"), annual compensation of \$1.2 million for an orthopedic surgeon serving as Medical Director in the Southwest region significantly exceeds established benchmarks. The 50th percentile for this role and specialty in the applicable geographic region is approximately \$750,000, and the 90th percentile is approximately \$1,050,000. Accordingly, the proposed \$1.2 million compensation exceeds the 90th percentile by approximately \$150,000, or roughly 14%. While there may be legitimate business reasons for offering compensation at or above the 90th percentile --- including the strategic importance of retaining Dr. Vasquez as the founder and the physician most closely identified with the Pinnacle brand --- compensation that exceeds the 90th percentile of nationally recognized survey data places a heavy burden on the parties to demonstrate fair market value through an independent, contemporaneous valuation.

**Regulatory Framework.** Under the Stark Law (42 U.S.C. §1395nn), physician self-referral of designated health services to an entity with which the physician (or an immediate family member) has a financial relationship is prohibited unless the arrangement satisfies an applicable exception. For compensation arrangements, the most commonly relied-upon exceptions are the employment exception (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(e)(2)) and the personal services arrangement exception (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(e)(3)). Each of these exceptions requires, among other conditions, that the compensation paid to the physician be consistent with fair market value and not be determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals by the referring physician. Compensation that exceeds established FMV benchmarks raises a presumption that the excess compensation may be attributable to the physician\'s referral activity rather than the fair market value of the services actually rendered.

Under the Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. §1320a-7b(b)), the knowing and willful offer, payment, solicitation, or receipt of remuneration to induce or reward referrals of items or services payable by federal healthcare programs is a criminal offense punishable by up to ten years\' imprisonment and fines of up to \$100,000 per occurrence, as well as mandatory exclusion from federal healthcare programs. The employment safe harbor (42 C.F.R. §1001.952(i)) provides protection for bona fide employment arrangements, but requires that the compensation be consistent with fair market value for the services actually performed by the employee. Compensation that exceeds FMV benchmarks is a recognized red flag for AKS enforcement, particularly in the context of private equity-backed healthcare transactions, which have been the subject of increasing OIG scrutiny.

**Significance for This Transaction.** Dr. Vasquez is the founder and majority shareholder (58%) of Pinnacle. He is an orthopedic surgeon who generates substantial referral volume for designated health services reimbursable by federal healthcare programs, including MRI imaging, laboratory services, and physical therapy --- each of which is furnished through ancillary arrangements discussed in Section IV.C below. Pinnacle derives approximately 51% of its revenue (\$95.53 million) from federal healthcare programs. The magnitude of referrals flowing from Dr. Vasquez, combined with compensation exceeding the 90th percentile of nationally recognized benchmarks, creates a pattern that the OIG has specifically identified as a compliance risk in private equity-backed healthcare transactions. The OIG\'s October 2023 Special Fraud Alert regarding physician compensation arrangements in corporate practice contexts specifically cautioned against compensation structures that exceed fair mar

ket value and may serve as a mechanism for compensating physicians for their referral activity.

**Additional Context.** In addition to the proposed \$1.2 million annual compensation, Dr. Vasquez is rolling over approximately \$26.0 million in equity as part of the merger consideration. The combination of above-FMV employment compensation and significant rollover equity participation warrants careful structuring to ensure that all compensation elements --- including salary, benefits, bonuses, and equity --- when considered in the aggregate, satisfy fair market value requirements under both the Stark Law and the AKS. The equity rollover itself must be structured at fair market value and on terms that do not take into account the volume or value of referrals.

**Recommendation.** We recommend the following: (a) require an independent, third-party fair market value opinion from a qualified healthcare valuation firm (such as VMG Health or HealthCare Appraisers) before signing, covering all elements of Dr. Vasquez\'s post-closing compensation, including salary, bonus opportunity, benefits, and the rollover equity; (b) if the FMV opinion does not support compensation at the \$1.2 million level, the employment agreement must be renegotiated to bring total compensation within the 75th percentile or lower of applicable benchmarks, absent compelling, documented justification for a higher level; (c) include a contractual commitment to annual FMV reviews of Dr. Vasquez\'s compensation during the employment term; and (d) include in the merger agreement a specific representation by Seller that all post-closing physician compensation arrangements have been structured to comply with the Stark Law and AKS, with a corresponding indemnification obligation for any breach.

**[IV.B. Related-Party Lease Arrangements --- Stark/AKS Overlay]{.underline}**

Three of Pinnacle\'s Texas clinic locations are leased from Vasquez Medical Properties LLC, a single-member limited liability company owned personally by Dr. Raymond Vasquez. The annual rental payments under these three leases are as follows: \$420,000 for the first location, \$385,000 for the second location, and \$510,000 for the third location, for a total annual rental obligation of \$1.315 million. According to the preliminary real estate analysis conducted by Ridgeline Capital Advisors and corroborated in the Thornfield Advisory Group Quality of Earnings report, the aggregate rental payments under these three leases exceed fair market rental rates for comparable commercial medical office space in the applicable submarkets by approximately 22%.

**Stark Law Concern.** The Stark Law rental exception (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(e)(1)(A)) permits a physician to have a financial relationship with an entity to which the physician makes referrals, provided that the lease arrangement meets specified conditions. Among the most critical requirements is that the rental charges over the term of the lease are set in advance, are consistent with fair market value, and are not determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals. Rental payments that are 22% above fair market value to an entity controlled by a referring physician who generates substantial federal healthcare program referrals present a significant compliance concern. On their face, above-FMV rental payments to a physician-controlled entity do not satisfy the fair market value requirement of the rental exception and therefore expose Pinnacle to potential Stark Law violations for all designated health services referred by Dr. Vasquez at those three clinic locations.

**AKS Concern.** The Anti-Kickback Statute space rental safe harbor (42 C.F.R. §1001.952(b)) similarly requires that aggregate rental payments be consistent with fair market value for the space rented and not take into account the volume or value of referrals. Above-FMV rental payments to a physician who refers patients for federally reimbursable services constitute potential illegal remuneration under the AKS.

This finding intersects with the financial due diligence findings in the Thornfield Advisory Group Quality of Earnings report and the lease summary schedule prepared by Ridgeline Capital Advisors. The regulatory concern amplifies the economic overpayment concern by adding potential Stark Law and AKS liability to the cost of the above-FMV lease arrangements.

**Recommendation.** The draft merger agreement should require renegotiation of the three Vasquez Medical Properties LLC leases to fair market rental rates as a pre-closing covenant or closing condition. Alternatively, Buyer should negotiate to terminate these leases and enter into direct leases with the underlying landlords, or acquire the underlying real estate from Vasquez Medical Properties LLC at fair market value. An independent commercial real estate appraisal should be obtained to establish FMV rental rates for each of the three clinic locations. Any continuing lease arrangement with a Vasquez-affiliated entity post-closing must be supported by a contemporaneous, independent FMV appraisal.

**[IV.C. Ancillary Services Arrangements --- In-Office Ancillary Services Exception]{.underline}**

**Finding.** Pinnacle has entered into exclusive ancillary services agreements for MRI imaging, clinical laboratory, and physical therapy services with entities in which Dr. Vasquez holds ownership interests. These arrangements have been structured to rely on the Stark Law in-office ancillary services (\"IOAS\") exception (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(b)(2)), which permits physician self-referral for certain designated health services when those services are furnished within the physician\'s group practice and meet specific conditions regarding supervision, location, and billing.

**MRI and Laboratory Services.** Based on our review, the MRI imaging services and clinical laboratory services subject to these ancillary agreements appear to be furnished within the same buildings in which Pinnacle\'s referring physicians provide physician services. Subject to confirmation that the other requirements of the IOAS exception are satisfied --- including the supervision requirement (that the services are furnished under the supervision of a physician who is a member of the group practice), the billing requirement (that the services are billed by the group practice or by an entity wholly owned by the group practice), and the group practice requirements of 42 C.F.R. §411.352 --- these MRI and laboratory arrangements appear facially compliant with the IOAS exception. We recommend, however, that a detailed IOAS compliance checklist be completed for each service line to confirm satisfaction of all applicable regulatory conditions.

**Physical Therapy Services --- Critical Issue.** The physical therapy services are provided at a separate, standalone facility located approximately two miles from Pinnacle\'s main clinic location. This physical therapy facility is operated by an entity in which Dr. Vasquez holds a partial ownership interest. The IOAS exception contains strict location requirements. Specifically, designated health services must be provided either:

> \(a\) in the \"same building\" in which the referring physician furnishes physician services unrelated to the furnishing of designated health services (42 C.F.R. §411.355(b)(2)(i)(A)); or
>
> \(b\) in a \"centralized building\" that is used by the group practice for the provision of some or all of the group practice\'s designated health services (42 C.F.R. §411.355(b)(2)(i)(B)).

**Analysis.** A standalone physical therapy facility located approximately two miles from the clinic at which Pinnacle\'s referring physicians see patients cannot satisfy the \"same building\" test. The regulations define \"same building\" as a structure that has a single street address, and the physical therapy facility is at a separate address entirely. For the \"centralized building\" alternative, the regulations contemplate a facility that is used by the group practice itself for the provision of some or all of its designated health services. A standalone physical therapy facility two miles from the main clinic, owned and operated by a separate entity (albeit one partially owned by Dr. Vasquez) rather than by the Pinnacle group practice, is unlikely to qualify as a \"centralized building\" under the regulatory framework. The centralized building concept was designed to accommodate situations in which a group practice consolidates its ancillary services at a central location that the group practice controls --- not situations in which designated health services are furnished by a separate, physician-owned entity at a remote location.

**Exposure.** If the IOAS exception does not apply to the physical therapy referrals, every self-referral by a Pinnacle physician to the off-site physical therapy entity constitutes a violation of the Stark Law. Under the Stark Law\'s strict liability framework, a violation triggers several consequences: (i) denial of payment and obligation to refund all amounts collected for the referred services (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(g)(2)); (ii) potential civil monetary penalties of up to \$15,000 per service furnished pursuant to a prohibited referral (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(g)(3)); and (iii) potential assessment of up to three times the amount claimed for each service (42 U.S.C. §1395nn(g)(3)). Additionally, claims submitted to federal healthcare programs for services furnished in violation of the Stark Law may give rise to liability under the False Claims Act. Because Dr. Vasquez holds an ownership interest in the physical therapy entity, the AKS is independently implicated: the referral of patients for federally reimbursable physical therapy services to an entity in which the referring physician has an ownership stake, without satisfying a recognized safe harbor, constitutes potential illegal remuneration.

**Quantification.** We have requested but not yet received complete billing data for the physical therapy referrals to the off-site location. Based on preliminary revenue estimates provided by Pinnacle\'s billing manager during our interview, the physical therapy services furnished at this location generate approximately \$2.8 million to \$3.5 million in annual revenue. Based on the Target\'s overall payer mix, a significant portion of this revenue --- estimated at 40% to 50% --- is reimbursed by federal healthcare programs. The refund exposure over the relevant lookback period (potentially up to six years under the FCA statute of limitations) could be substantial, likely in the range of \$3.4 million to \$10.5 million, exclusive of per-claim penalties and treble damages.

**Recommendation.** We recommend the following: (a) require Seller to provide complete billing records for the off-site physical therapy location, including claims-level data identifying each referring physician, the payer for each claim, and the amounts billed and collected; (b) engage experienced healthcare regulatory counsel to prepare a detailed Stark Law analysis, including evaluation of whether any alternative Stark exception (such as the fair market value exception at 42 C.F.R. §411.357(l)) could be satisfied; (c) as a structural matter, consider terminating the physical therapy arrangement prior to closing or restructuring it to bring it into compliance with an applicable Stark exception; (d) include a specific indemnity in the merger agreement for any Stark Law liability arising from the ancillary services arrangements, structured outside the general basket and cap; and (e) evaluate the impact of the physical therapy Stark exposure on the R&W insurance policy.

**[IV.D. Co-Management Agreement with St. Ambrose Regional Medical Center]{.underline}**

Pinnacle is party to a co-management agreement with St. Ambrose Regional Medical Center for the co-management of the hospital\'s orthopedic service line. Under this agreement, Pinnacle provides management, quality improvement, and clinical oversight services in exchange for a base management fee and performance-based incentive payments tied to certain operational and clinical metrics.

Our review of the co-management agreement indicates that the performance metrics used to calculate incentive compensation include both clinical quality measures (e.g., surgical site infection rates, patient satisfaction scores, readmission rates) and patient volume metrics (e.g., orthopedic case volume, outpatient visit growth). The inclusion of patient volume-based metrics in a compensation formula for a physician group that refers patients to the hospital for orthopedic services creates a significant AKS compliance risk. The personal services and management contracts safe harbor (42 C.F.R. §1001.952(d)) requires, among other conditions, that the aggregate compensation paid over the term of the agreement be set in advance, be consistent with fair market value, and not be determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals between the parties. Performance incentives tied to patient volume may be viewed by the OIG as a proxy for referral-based compensation.

We recommend obtaining an independent FMV opinion for the co-management agreement, with particular attention to the performance-based incentive compensation structure. The performance metrics should be reviewed to confirm they are not serving as proxies for referral volume, and we recommend restructuring the incentive payments to be based solely on quality and outcomes metrics, eliminating any volume-based components.

**[V.B. Dr. William \"Bo\" Hagerty --- Oklahoma Medical Board Warning]{.underline}**

**Finding.** Dr. William \"Bo\" Hagerty, a minority shareholder holding 10% of Pinnacle\'s equity, received an informal warning letter from the Oklahoma Medical Board in 2022 regarding inadequate documentation of controlled substance prescriptions. The warning letter, identified through our independent review of publicly available Oklahoma Medical Board records, cited deficiencies in Dr. Hagerty\'s documentation practices for Schedule II and Schedule III controlled substance prescriptions, including insufficient notation of the medical necessity for the prescribed substances, inadequate documentation of patient history and examination findings to support the prescribing decisions, and failure to maintain certain records required under Oklahoma Administrative Code Title 435, Chapter 10. No formal disciplinary action resulted from the warning letter, and Dr. Hagerty\'s Oklahoma medical license remains active and unrestricted.

**Due Diligence Discovery.** This matter was identified solely through our independent review of Oklahoma Medical Board public records and databases. It was not disclosed by Seller or Seller\'s counsel (Breckenridge Sloane LLP) at any point during the due diligence process. Specifically, Dr. Hagerty\'s credentialing file, as maintained and produced by Pinnacle, does not reference or include a copy of the 2022 warning letter. We did not locate any reference to the warning letter in Pinnacle\'s compliance program files, internal audit reports, or board or committee minutes. When we raised this matter with Janet Morales during our interview, she stated she was unaware of the warning letter and would need to consult with Dr. Hagerty.

**Draft Merger Agreement Representation.** The draft merger agreement circulated by Breckenridge Sloane LLP on January 8, 2025, contains a representation and warranty by Seller that, to Seller\'s knowledge, no physician employed by or affiliated with Pinnacle has been \"the subject of any investigation, inquiry, warning, or disciplinary action\" by any state medical licensing board during the five-year period preceding the signing date. Dr. Hagerty\'s 2022 informal warning from the Oklahoma Medical Board falls squarely within the scope of this representation, as the warning was issued within the relevant five-year lookback period, was directed at Dr. Hagerty in his capacity as a physician employed by and affiliated with Pinnacle, and constitutes both an \"inquiry\" and a \"warning\" within the plain meaning of those terms as used in the representation.

**Disclosure Schedule Gap.** The disclosure schedules circulated with the draft merger agreement --- specifically, the schedule designated for physician licensing matters --- do not disclose the Hagerty warning letter. This constitutes either (a) a breach of the seller\'s representation and warranty (if Seller had actual or constructive knowledge of the warning and failed to disclose it), or (b) an omission requiring prompt supplementation of the disclosure schedules before the representation can be accurately made at signing.

**Substantive Concern.** While an informal warning letter is a less severe regulatory action than formal discipline, suspension, or probation, the subject matter of the warning raises meaningful compliance concerns. The inadequate documentation of controlled substance prescribing in the pain management context is particularly noteworthy when considered alongside the separate overbilling findings in Pinnacle\'s pain management division discussed in Section III.B above. The convergence of documentation deficiencies in controlled substance prescribing and systematic upcoding of E&M services within the same clinical division suggests a pattern of lax documentation and compliance oversight that warrants heightened scrutiny by the Buyer. If Dr. Hagerty\'s prescribing documentation deficiencies have not been remediated, the continued prescribing practices could expose the surviving entity to DEA enforcement action, state medical board discipline, and potential liability under the Controlled Substances Act.

**Dr. Hagerty\'s Transaction Role.** Dr. Hagerty is rolling over approximately \$5.02 million in equity as part of the merger consideration. He is expected to continue as an employed physician post-closing. His compliance history is directly relevant to the ongoing regulatory posture of the surviving entity, and any undisclosed adverse licensing matter could affect payer credentialing, hospital privileging, and the entity\'s compliance profile with government programs.

**Recommendation.** We recommend the following: (a) require Seller to supplement the disclosure schedules immediately to include the 2022 Oklahoma Medical Board informal warning letter; (b) obtain a complete copy of the actual warning letter and any response submitted by Dr. Hagerty or on his behalf; (c) conduct a focused review of Dr. Hagerty\'s controlled substance prescribing patterns during the period from the 2022 warning through the present, including a review of prescription monitoring program data for both Texas and Oklahoma; (d) evaluate whether the failure to disclose this matter constitutes a breach of the seller\'s representation sufficient to trigger remedies under the merger agreement and to affect the R&W insurance policy (\$30 million limit, \$2.0 million retention); (e) consider requiring an in-person or remote interview of Dr. Hagerty by the Buyer\'s compliance team prior to signing to assess the circumstances of the warning and any remedial steps taken; and (f) review Dr. Hagerty\'s current credentialing status at all hospitals and facilities where he holds privileges to confirm no related restrictions.

**[VI. HIPAA Privacy and Security Compliance]{.underline}**

**[VI.A. August 2024 HIPAA Breach and OCR Investigation]{.underline}**

**Finding.** In August 2024, Pinnacle submitted a breach notification to the United States Department of Health and Human Services (\"HHS\") Office for Civil Rights (\"OCR\") regarding a security incident that exposed protected health information (\"PHI\") for approximately 3,200 individuals. The breach has been posted on the HHS Breach Portal (commonly referred to as the \"Wall of Shame\") and is publicly available.

**Nature of the Breach.** The breach resulted from a misconfiguration in Pinnacle\'s electronic patient portal. According to the documentation reviewed during due diligence, the misconfiguration permitted unauthorized individuals to access PHI through the patient-facing portal without proper authentication controls. The misconfiguration is reported to have been present for approximately six weeks before it was identified and remediated. The affected data included patient names, dates of birth, clinical diagnoses, treatment records, medication lists, and insurance information. No financial information (such as Social Security numbers or credit card numbers) is reported to have been exposed, although the breadth of clinical information compromised is significant from both a patient privacy and a regulatory enforcement perspective.

**Notification.** Pinnacle provided timely notification to affected individuals and to HHS/OCR as required under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subpart D). Individual notification letters were sent to the approximately 3,200 affected patients within sixty (60) days of the discovery of the breach. Because the breach affected more than 500 individuals in both Texas and Oklahoma, Pinnacle was also required to provide prominent media notice in each affected state, which it did. We reviewed copies of the notification letters and media notices, and they appear to comply with the content requirements of 45 C.F.R. §164.404.

**OCR Investigation Status.** OCR has opened a compliance review in connection with the reported breach. As of the date of this memorandum, the investigation remains open. No resolution agreement, corrective action plan, or civil money penalty has been assessed. OCR correspondence reviewed during due diligence indicates that OCR has requested, among other items, Pinnacle\'s most recent HIPAA security risk analysis, its HIPAA policies and procedures, evidence of workforce HIPAA training, and documentation of the remedial measures implemented following the breach. Pinnacle\'s IT security officer confirmed during our interview that responses to OCR\'s requests are being prepared but have not yet been submitted. The incomplete status of Pinnacle\'s responses to OCR increases the risk that the investigation will extend beyond the anticipated closing date and potentially beyond the expected March 15, 2025 signing date.

**Potential Penalties.** Under HIPAA\'s tiered penalty structure, as set forth in 45 C.F.R. §160.404, civil money penalties are assessed on a per-violation basis and range from \$137 to \$68,928 per violation (as adjusted for inflation), depending on the level of culpability. The annual cap for each violation category is approximately \$2.07 million. For purposes of HIPAA enforcement, each affected individual may constitute a separate violation. For 3,200 affected records, even at the lowest penalty tier (Tier 1, reflecting a violation the covered entity did not know about and would not have known about through the exercise of reasonable diligence), the poten

tial penalty would be approximately \$438,400. At higher tiers reflecting reasonable cause or willful neglect, penalties escalate significantly and could reach the annual cap. If OCR determines that the misconfiguration reflected a systemic failure to implement adequate security safeguards --- particularly in light of the fact that Pinnacle\'s most recent HIPAA security risk analysis was conducted internally in 2021 and no independent assessment has ever been performed --- penalties at Tier 3 (willful neglect, corrected) or Tier 4 (willful neglect, not corrected) levels are possible.

**Remediation and Litigation Costs.** In addition to potential OCR civil money penalties, Pinnacle may incur substantial costs for credit monitoring services offered to affected individuals (though the absence of financial data in the breach may mitigate this cost), ongoing forensic investigation and security remediation, legal defense costs, and potential private litigation. Class action lawsuits following healthcare data breaches have become increasingly common, and the exposure of clinical diagnoses and treatment records may give rise to claims for emotional distress and invasion of privacy. We are not aware of any class action or individual litigation filed against Pinnacle in connection with the August 2024 breach as of the date of this memorandum, but the statute of limitations for such claims would not have expired.

**Draft Merger Agreement Gaps.** The draft merger agreement, as circulated on January 8, 2025, does not include: (a) resolution or satisfactory status of the OCR investigation as a closing condition or as a bring-down condition at closing; (b) a specific indemnity for potential HIPAA fines, remediation costs, credit monitoring expenses, and related litigation expenses arising from the August 2024 breach; or (c) a requirement that Pinnacle maintain adequate cyber liability insurance coverage through closing and for a reasonable tail period. Under the current indemnification framework, any HIPAA-related losses would fall under the general representations and warranties regarding compliance with applicable law, subject to the \$1.5 million deductible basket and the general indemnification cap of 10% of equity value (approximately \$19.51 million). Given the potential magnitude of the OCR penalties, remediation costs, and litigation exposure --- and the fact that this is a known, pre-closing matter --- reliance on the general indemnification framework is inadequate.

**Recommendation.** We recommend the following actions: (a) negotiate a specific indemnity for all losses arising from or related to the August 2024 HIPAA breach, structured from dollar one and outside the general basket and cap; (b) consider requiring resolution of the OCR investigation (or, at minimum, receipt of a materially favorable status update or indication of a likely resolution range) as a condition to closing; (c) engage a qualified third-party cybersecurity firm to conduct an independent security assessment of Pinnacle\'s IT infrastructure, including its patient portal, electronic health record system, and network security controls, prior to closing; (d) evaluate whether the R&W insurance policy covers pre-closing HIPAA breach liabilities --- as a known matter, this exposure is likely excluded from coverage; (e) verify that Pinnacle maintains adequate cyber liability insurance with sufficient limits to cover the potential exposure, and require that any such policy include a tail period extending beyond the closing date; and (f) require Pinnacle to submit its complete response to OCR\'s pending data requests before the expiration of the due diligence period on February 28, 2025.

**[VI.B. General HIPAA Compliance Posture]{.underline}**

Beyond the August 2024 breach and OCR investigation, our review of Pinnacle\'s general HIPAA compliance posture revealed several observations. Pinnacle maintains written HIPAA privacy and security policies and procedures, last updated in 2022. The designated Privacy Officer is Janet Morales, who concurrently serves as Vice President of Human Resources and part-time Chief Compliance Officer --- adding a third hat to her already overburdened role. Annual workforce HIPAA training has been conducted, and we reviewed attendance records and training materials for the 2023 and 2024 training sessions, which appear adequate in scope and content.

The most significant deficiency in Pinnacle\'s HIPAA compliance posture, beyond the breach itself, is the absence of a current, independent HIPAA security risk analysis. The most recent security risk analysis was conducted internally in 2021 --- approximately three and a half years ago. No independent, third-party security risk analysis has ever been performed. The HIPAA Security Rule (45 C.F.R. §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)) requires covered entities to conduct an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of electronic PHI. OCR enforcement actions have consistently emphasized the importance of regular, thorough risk analyses, and the absence of a current risk analysis is frequently cited as a contributing factor in breach-related enforcement actions.

Business Associate Agreements are in place with Pinnacle\'s major vendors, including Apex Practice Solutions LLC (which provides revenue cycle management and billing services) and the electronic health record system vendor. We reviewed a sample of BAAs and they appear to contain the required provisions under 45 C.F.R. §164.314(a).

We recommend that, post-closing, Buyer engage a qualified third-party firm to conduct an independent, comprehensive HIPAA security risk analysis and update all HIPAA policies and procedures to address identified vulnerabilities.

**[VII. Immigration Compliance --- J-1 Visa Waiver Physicians]{.underline}**

**Finding.** Four (4) of Pinnacle\'s sixty-two (62) employed physicians are currently practicing under J-1 visa waivers with remaining service obligations at designated Health Professional Shortage Area (\"HPSA\") sites. These physicians were recruited to Pinnacle under the Conrad 30 State program or a related Interested Government Agency (\"IGA\") J-1 waiver program.

**J-1 Visa Waiver Program Overview.** Under the J-1 visa waiver programs, foreign medical graduates who have completed graduate medical education in the United States on J-1 exchange visitor visas are ordinarily subject to a two-year home residency requirement before they may change to another nonimmigrant status (such as H-1B) or obtain lawful permanent residence. The Conrad 30 program and IGA waiver programs provide a mechanism for waiving this two-year requirement if the physician agrees to practice full-time clinical medicine in a designated HPSA or Medically Underserved Area (\"MUA\") for a period of not less than three years. These service obligations are tied to specific employers, specific practice locations, and specific HPSA or MUA designations. Any material change in the physician\'s employer, practice location, or scope of clinical practice --- including a reduction in clinical hours at the designated HPSA site --- may jeopardize the physician\'s immigration status and trigger the two-year home residency requirement.

**Specific Risks from the Merger.** The proposed reverse triangular merger presents several specific risks to the J-1 waiver physicians\' immigration status and compliance:

> **(a) Change of Employer.** Although the reverse triangular merger structure results in Pinnacle surviving as the employer of record, the change in ultimate ownership --- from physician shareholders to a private equity-controlled acquisition subsidiary --- may be viewed by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (\"USCIS\") as a material change in the employment relationship. Depending on how USCIS evaluates the transaction, the merger may constitute a \"successor-in-interest\" change that requires notification to USCIS, amendment of the J-1 waiver documentation, or filing of new H-1B petitions (if the physicians have transitioned from J-1 to H-1B status). Failure to properly notify USCIS of a material change in the employment relationship could jeopardize the waiver status and expose the physicians to potential removal proceedings.
>
> **(b) Practice Site Changes.** If Buyer exercises its post-closing discretion to close, consolidate, or relocate clinics --- particularly clinics located in HPSA-designated areas --- the J-1 waiver physicians may be unable to fulfill their three-year service obligations at the designated HPSA sites. A physician who fails to complete the required three-year service period at the designated location is in violation of the waiver conditions and may be subject to reinstatement of the two-year home residency requirement. This risk is particularly acute if any of the four J-1 physicians are located at clinics that may be subject to lease non-renewal or relocation for business reasons.
>
> **(c) Physician Flight Risk.** If the J-1 waiver physicians become concerned about their immigration status as a result of the change of ownership --- whether due to uncertainty about the continuing HPSA designation, potential clinic closures, or changes in clinical operations --- they may seek alternative employment with another HPSA-designated employer to preserve their waiver eligibility. The departure of even one physician from a HPSA-designated clinic could have downstream consequences beyond the loss of the individual physician. In some cases, the departure of a physician from a HPSA site may affect the site\'s HPSA score or designation, which in turn could affect other J-1 waiver physicians at the same site and could impact the clinic\'s eligibility for enhanced Medicare reimbursement rates available to HPSA-qualifying sites.

**Information Gaps.** We have requested but not yet received the following information from Seller and Seller\'s counsel: (i) the specific HPSA sites at which each of the four J-1 waiver physicians is fulfilling his or her service obligation; (ii) the remaining duration of each physician\'s three-year service obligation (i.e., the date on which each physician\'s three-year period commenced and the expected completion date); (iii) copies of the J-1 waiver applications, approval notices, and any related correspondence with the sponsoring state agency or federal IGA; (iv) the identity of the sponsoring agency (state Department of Health, federal IGA, or other) for each waiver; and (v) the current immigration status of each physician (J-1, H-1B, or adjustment of status pending). These information gaps must be addressed before the due diligence expiration date of February 28, 2025.

**Draft Merger Agreement.** The draft merger agreement circulated on January 8, 2025 does not address immigration compliance, J-1 visa waiver obligations, or the continuation of HPSA site designations post-closing. There are no representations or warranties specifically addressing the immigration status of Pinnacle\'s workforce. There are no covenants restricting the Buyer from closing or relocating HPSA-designated clinic sites during the pendency of J-1 waiver service obligations. The absence of any immigration-related provisions in the draft agreement is a significant gap that must be addressed before signing.

**Recommendation.** We recommend the following: (a) obtain complete immigration files for all four J-1 waiver physicians, including waiver applications, approval notices, employment authorization documents, and any amendments or correspondence with USCIS or the sponsoring agency; (b) engage experienced immigration counsel to assess whether the reverse triangular merger structure triggers notification, re-filing, or amendment requirements with USCIS with respect to the J-1 waiver physicians; (c) include a specific representation in the merger agreement regarding the immigration status of all Pinnacle employees, with particular disclosure of the four J-1 waiver physicians, their designated HPSA practice sites, and the remaining duration of their service obligations; (d) include a covenant in the merger agreement restricting Buyer from closing, consolidating, or relocating any HPSA-designated clinic site during the pendency of any J-1 waiver service obligation without first obtaining immigration counsel approval and ensuring continuity of the waiver conditions; (e) cross-reference the J-1 physician practice locations with the Plano and Frisco clinic lease expiration dates to evaluate whether any of the four J-1 physicians are located at clinics with near-term lease expirations or potential closure risk; and (f) incorporate J-1 physician retention and immigration compliance into the post-closing integration plan.

**[VIII. Medicare/Medicaid Change of Ownership (CHOW) Considerations]{.underline}**

Pinnacle holds active Medicare provider enrollment for each of its fourteen (14) clinic locations. Under 42 C.F.R. §489.18, a change of ownership of a Medicare-enrolled provider or supplier requires the provider to submit a CHOW notification to the applicable Medicare Administrative Contractor (\"MAC\") and to CMS. A \"change of ownership\" for purposes of Medicare enrollment includes, among other events, a merger in which the provider is the surviving entity but its ownership structure changes. The proposed reverse triangular merger, in which Pinnacle will survive as a wholly owned subsidiary of Clearview, constitutes a change of ownership triggering CHOW notification obligations.

For the three Oklahoma clinic locations that participate in the Oklahoma SoonerSelect Medicaid managed care program, CHOW notifications will also be required to the Oklahoma Health Care Authority (\"OHCA\") and to each SoonerSelect managed care organization with which Pinnacle holds a participating provider agreement. The SoonerSelect MCO contracts may contain assignment and change-of-control provisions that impose additional requirements, such as prior written consent from the MCO, notification within specified timeframes, or re-credentialing of providers following the change of ownership.

The CHOW filings should be submitted promptly after closing, within the timeframes specified by each program. For Medicare, the MAC typically requires a completed CMS-855A or CMS-855B change of information form and supporting documentation (including the executed merger agreement and evidence of the change of ownership) within the time specified in the applicable program integrity guidelines. Failure to timely file CHOW applications could result in claims processing delays, claims denials, or, in extreme cases, termination of provider agreements --- any of which would have material adverse consequences for an entity deriving 51% of revenue from government payers.

The reverse triangular merger structure in which Pinnacle survives as the operating entity is generally favorable for CHOW purposes, because the surviving entity retains its Tax Identification Number, National Provider Identifiers, and Medicare provider enrollment numbers. This avoids the more complex and time-consuming process of new enrollment that would be required if the transaction were structured as an asset acquisition or a forward merger in which Pinnacle did not survive. However, the change in ultimate beneficial ownership --- from physician shareholders to a private equity-controlled entity --- nonetheless triggers the CHOW obligation and may invite additional scrutiny from CMS or the MAC regarding the ownership and management structure of the surviving entity.

We recommend that CHOW applications be prepared in advance and filed immediately upon closing. Coordination with the applicable CMS regional offices, the MAC, OHCA, and the SoonerSelect MCOs should begin prior to closing to minimize the risk of enrollment gaps or claims processing disruptions.

**Immediate Actions Required Before the February 28, 2025 Due Diligence Expiration Deadline:**

1\. **Physical therapy billing data.** Submit a formal request to Seller\'s counsel for complete billing records for the off-site physical therapy location, including claims-level data identifying referring physicians, payers, and amounts billed and collected, for the full period of the arrangement.

2\. **J-1 physician immigration files.** Submit a formal request for complete immigration files for all four J-1 visa waiver physicians, including waiver applications, approval notices, sponsoring agency identification, practice site HPSA designations, and remaining service obligation periods.

3\. **Dr. Hagerty warning letter.** Request the actual 2022 Oklahoma Medical Board informal warning letter and any response submitted by or on behalf of Dr. Hagerty, as well as any follow-up correspondence or monitoring requirements imposed by the Board.

4\. **OCR correspondence.** Request all OCR correspondence received by Pinnacle following the August 2024 breach notification, including the data requests issued by OCR and drafts of Pinnacle\'s responses (to the extent not privileged).

5\. **Dr. Vasquez-affiliated entities.** Request ownership documentation for all entities in which Dr. Vasquez holds an interest, including Vasquez Medical Properties LLC and the entities operating the MRI, laboratory, and physical therapy services, together with complete copies of all ancillary services agreements.

**Items to Address in Merger Agreement Negotiations (Ahead of Expected March 15, 2025 Signing):**

1\. **Specific indemnities.** Negotiate specific indemnification provisions, from dollar one and outside the general basket and cap, for: (a) the \$1.8 million overbilling/upcoding exposure in the pain management division, including all costs of voluntary self-disclosure and settlement; (b) all losses arising from the August 2024 HIPAA breach and OCR investigation, including fines, remediation costs, and litigation defense and settlement costs; and (c) any Stark Law liability arising from the ancillary services arrangements, including the off-site physical therapy referrals.

2\. **Disclosure schedule supplementation.** Require Seller to supplement the disclosure schedules immediately to include the 2022 Oklahoma Medical Board informal warning letter regarding Dr. Hagerty.

3\. **Pre-closing covenants.** Negotiate pre-closing covenants requiring Seller to: (a) initiate a voluntary self-disclosure of the pain management overbilling to the OIG under its Self-Disclosure Protocol prior to closing (or, at minimum, prior to a date certain post-closing, with corresponding escrow); and (b) renegotiate the three Vasquez Medical Properties LLC leases to fair market rental rates, supported by an independent appraisal.

4\. **Closing conditions.** Negotiate the following as conditions to Buyer\'s obligation to close: (a) satisfactory resolution or status update of the OCR investigation relating to the August 2024 HIPAA breach; (b) receipt of an independent, third-party fair market value opinion supporting Dr. Vasquez\'s post-closing compensation; and (c) completion of an independent coding audit of the pain management division by a qualified third-party compliance firm.

5\. **Post-closing covenants.** Include covenants requiring the surviving entity to: (a) maintain all J-1 waiver physicians at their designated HPSA practice sites for the duration of their respective service obligations; and (b) appoint a full-time, independent Chief Compliance Officer within ninety (90) days following closing.

**Coordination with Other Advisors.** We recommend coordinating with Ridgeline Capital Advisors and Thornfield Advisory Group to ensure that the financial implications of the regulatory findings described in this memorandum --- including the potential \$1.8 million overbilling refund, the \$1.315 million above-FMV lease overpayment, the off-site physical therapy Stark exposure, and the HIPAA breach costs --- are reflected in the Quality of Earnings analysis and the transaction financial model.

**Next Call.** We recommend scheduling a call with Margaret Yoon and Karen Chu at the earliest opportunity to discuss prioritization of the action items above, allocation of responsibilities among the deal team, and the strategy for presenting these findings to Seller\'s counsel in the context of the ongoing merger agreement negotiations.

This memorandum is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. It is intended solely for use by Clearview Health Partners LLC and its authorized representatives in connection with the proposed acquisition of Pinnacle Medical Group, P.A. Do not distribute without prior authorization from Linden, Ashby & Whitmore LLP.

Linden, Ashby & Whitmore LLP 3100 McKinney Avenue, Suite 2400 Dallas, TX 75201

Under §2.5, the P.A. then converts within 30 days into a Texas business corporation, “Pinnacle Medical Group, Inc.” Under §2.6, Karen Chu and David Prescott, who are not physicians, become directors and Chairman.",

Only physicians may own, and generally only physicians may serve as governing persons of, a professional association formed to practice medicine (TBOC Chapters 301 and 302). A lay entity may not practice medicine, employ physicians to practice medicine, or control a physician’s medical judgment (see, e.g., Tex. Occ. Code §§155.001, 164.052 (aiding and abetting the unlicensed practice of medicine) and Texas Medical Board rules). The structure in the draft therefore fails at three separate points: (i) a non-physician Parent holding 100% of the P.A.’s equity; (ii) non-physician directors under §2.6 and a business-corporation charter under §2.4; and (iii) a converted business corporation that would employ the 62 physicians and 41 APPs and bill for professional services. "title": "Intended IRC §368(a) reorganization treatment is not available; no tax opinion; Buyer forgoes a basis step-up",
